 Jenny McCarthy Discards Wardrobe After Mold Exposure 
 Jenny McCarthy Discards Wardrobe After Mold Exposure

 Jenny McCarthy and Donnie Wahlberg in Los Angeles in 2026. Credit: Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty

 Actress Jenny McCarthy and her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, have discarded their clothing and furniture after a serious mold exposure incident affected their health and forced them to leave their Los Angeles home. McCarthy discussed the financial and emotional consequences during a Tuesday episode of The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show.
 The actress explained that she lost decades of personal belongings, including clothing associated with important professional milestones and red carpet appearances. She also revealed that the experience has made her reluctant to purchase expensive replacements.

 McCarthy described the extent of the losses during her conversation with autoimmune disease specialist Amy Myers.

 "I wound up throwing everything away," McCarthy said.
 She explained that she had only recently purchased a new outfit because she no longer had an adequate wardrobe. Until then, she had been ordering inexpensive replacement clothing through TikTok Shop.
 "Literally, this is the first outfit I went and bought last night because I didn't have any clothes. I've been wearing clothes from TikTok shop. I'm on TikTok, I'll order something and send it. And that's what I wear," McCarthy said.
 Also Read 
 Stacy Keach Dies at 85 After Long Acting Career 
 The actress also described how losing her belongings had changed her attitude toward shopping and preserving personal memories.
 "I'm afraid to spend money on clothes anymore, because I had to give everything away. I'm like, that's 30 years of clothes, of red carpet events and memories," McCarthy said.
 The cleanup extended beyond her personal wardrobe. McCarthy said Wahlberg, whom she married in 2014, also had to dispose of his clothing because of concerns about continued contamination.
 Also Read

 "Now, I had to try to convince my husband that, 'Guess what? Your clothes also have to go bye-bye,'" McCarthy said.
 McCarthy previously described the psychological effects of the experience in October, saying that even after months of detoxification, she remained uncomfortable living in another property.
 "In month seven of detox," McCarthy said, she felt "too paranoid to honestly live anywhere else other than a tent."

 Dax Shepard Rejects Abuse Claims Against His Marriage 
 The couple also abandoned their household furniture when they moved out of their Los Angeles residence. McCarthy said she suspected the contamination might have originated in her makeup room because her makeup artist had also become seriously ill.
 "We left all of our furniture behind," McCarthy said.
 She explained that uncertainty about the source of the exposure influenced her decision to leave everything behind.
 Also Read 
 Morgan Freeman Shares His Approach to Aging and Acting 
 "Even though I believe my mold poisoning came from my makeup room, because my makeup artist got very sick with me," McCarthy said.
 Her concerns remained despite her uncertainty about where the contamination originated.
 "Still, I didn't want to risk anything," McCarthy said.
 Also Read 
 Katt Williams Reveals Childhood Abuse in New Memoir 
 Beyond losing personal possessions, McCarthy described the physical and emotional demands of her recovery. She said her treatment routine involved taking approximately 100 pills daily.
 "I find myself crying sometimes," McCarthy said.
 She also described the difficulty of managing the medication schedule.
 "100 pills a day. It's too much, and I'm gagging," McCarthy said.
 In March, McCarthy had detailed a range of health problems following what she described as six months of severe illness. Her reported symptoms included an infected root canal, pus-filled growths on her eyelids and mouth infections.
 She connected those health problems to what she identified as mycotoxin poisoning.
 "Six months of living hell," McCarthy said.
 She also described the condition using the term associated with exposure to toxins produced by mold and other fungi.
 "Mycotoxin poisoning," McCarthy said.
 According to the Cleveland Clinic, exposure to mycotoxins can affect the esophagus, stomach, intestines, eyes and mouth. The institution also identifies potential links with chronic illness and increased risks of asthma and cancer.
 The Cleveland Clinic recommends appropriately disposing of contaminated materials to reduce the potential spread of mycotoxins.
 Its guidance advises people to "properly [dispose] of anything they contaminate," according to the Cleveland Clinic.
